chunks: And among its changes is that you see the pitiable man becoming enviable, and the enviable man becoming pitiable,
This is because the wealth has gone and misfortune has come to him.
And among its lessons is that a man reaches near (the realization of) his desires when (suddenly) the approach of his death cuts them; then neither the desire is achieved nor the desires spared.
Glory to Allāh, how deceitful are its pleasures, how thirst-rousing its quenching and how sunny its shade. That which approaches (i.e. death) cannot be sent back, he who goes away does not return.
Glory to Allāh, how near is the living to the dead because he will meet him soon and how far is the dead from the living because he has gone away from him!

key_terms.الْمَرْحُومُ: The pitiable one (often referring to the poor or humble)
key_terms.الْمَغْبُوطُ: The enviable one (often referring to the wealthy or successful)

ai.seo_question: What are the key lessons about the transient nature of worldly life and death in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) employs the rhetorical device of *mughayara* (contrast) to illustrate the paradoxical nature of the deceased and the living, a theme deeply resonant in Shia *adab al-mawt* (etiquette of death) literature. This passage serves as a spiritual wake-up call, urging believers to recognize that worldly success is fleeting while the hereafter is the ultimate destination, thereby reinforcing the Shia emphasis on *zuhd* (asceticism) not as renunciation, but as detachment from the ephemeral to secure eternal success.
